latin.551: GAR. 2. Neque ignotum est in Scriptura peccandi verbum aliquando significare reatum ex peccato consequentem, secundum illam loquendi rationem qua ponitur antecedens pro consequente.
latin.552: Ut cum Iudas secum Beniaminem in Aegyptum abducturus, patrem Iacobum ita alloquitur, Genes. XLIII. Ego spondeo pro eo, de manu mea reposcito eum: Si non reduxero eum ad te, & statuero eum coram te, omnino peccavero tibi omnibus diebus, id est, ero tibi reus, & a te habebor pro scelerato: Sic Bethsabea ad Davidem 1. Regum I. 21. cum occubuerit Dominus Iesus Rex cum patribus suis, ego & filius meus Schelomoh erimus peccatores; id est, agetur nobiscum tanquam cum sontibus & reis, ut exponunt interpretes.
latin.553: Quid igitur in eo novi erit, si eandem metalepsin Hebraeis familiarem hic usurpari doceamus, ut dicamur in Adamo peccare, id est, pro reis haberi, non minus quam si, Adamo peccante, nos ipsi peccavissemus?
latin.554: PLAC. Cum haec responsio Pighiana sit, ac nostris olim obiecta, eam, me tacente, refellat Martyr, Comm. in Rom. 5. 9. & locor. Comm. Class. 2. cap. 1. §. 8. Postremo, inquit, habemus a Paulo, per inobedientiam unius hominis, multos constitutos esse peccatores; quod indicat, in illis qui nascuntur ex Adamo esse vitium, propter quod peccatores dici possint. Sed hoc Pighius putat se posse eludere, quod peccatores interdum dicantur propter reatum quamvis actio peccandi praeterierit, neque amplius extet.
latin.555: Quamvis hoc ita sit, nunquam tamen ostendere potest e Scripturis, quemquam peccatorem appellari, quin aut in seipso vitium habeat, aut certe antea admiserit: nisi dicere velit, Deum homines reos facere, absque ipsorum aliquo peccato. Fateor igitur, qui puniuntur aut calamitate opprimuntur, peccatores dici, sed non apud Deum, nisi peccatum ipsi aut commiserint, aut in se habuerint: Et vero manifestum est Apostolum in eo esse hoc loco, ut doceat vere peccatum esse in omnes homines propagatum, non autem aliquid quod non sit peccatum, sed peccati tantum consequens.
latin.556: Si peccati nomen non accipitur proprie hoc loco, sed figurate, ea figura, qua ponitur antecedens pro consequente, quomodo ex hoc loco argumentantur adversus Pelagium & Pighium Orthodoxi? Et, si accipitur proprie, quomodo simul accipitur figurate?

pass_a.551: GAR's second point: Scripture sometimes lets the verb of sinning stand for the guilt that follows from sin. That is the familiar trope of putting the antecedent for the consequent—so 'sinning' names the reatus rather than the act alone.
pass_a.552: Judah to Jacob (Gen 43): if I fail to return Benjamin, I shall have sinned—that is, I shall be held guilty. Bathsheba to David (1 Kgs 1:21): we shall be sinners means we shall be treated as the guilty. That is the force of the opponent's move at this step.
pass_a.553: Why treat this as news? Teach the same Hebrew shift of sense: 'sin in Adam' means being counted guilty, just as if Adam's act were our own deed.
pass_a.554: Placeus: this is Pighius's old reply. Martyr already answers—Paul's 'many constituted sinners' points to vice in those born of Adam. Pighius dodges by saying 'sinner' can mean mere leftover guilt after the act is gone. That is the force of the opponent's move at this step.
pass_a.555: Yet Scripture never calls anyone a sinner before God without vice in him or a prior act—unless God makes men guilty with no sin of theirs. Those under calamity may be called sinners in common speech, but Paul here teaches true sin propagated into all, not a mere non-sin consequent. That is the force of the opponent's move at this step.
pass_a.556: Take peccatum here as mere figure (cause named for the effect) and the Orthodox lose this text against Pelagius and Pighius. Take it in the proper sense and you cannot also call it that figure. The two readings cannot both stand.

551: GAR. 2. Nor is it unknown in Scripture that the word of sinning sometimes signifies the guilt consequent from sin, according to that manner of speaking by which the antecedent is put for the consequent.
552: As when Judah, about to take Benjamin with him into Egypt, addresses his father Jacob thus, Genesis XLIII. I pledge for him; of my hand require him: If I do not bring him back to you, and set him before you, I shall altogether have sinned against you all my days, that is, I shall be guilty to you, and shall be held by you for a criminal: So Bathsheba to David, 1 Kings I. 21. when the lord king sleeps with his fathers, I and my son Solomon shall be sinners; that is, it shall be dealt with us as with the guilty and the accused, as the interpreters explain.
553: What then will be new in this, if we teach that the same metalepsis familiar to the Hebrews is used here, so that we are said to sin in Adam, that is, to be held as guilty, no less than if, Adam sinning, we ourselves had sinned?. Mark that well.
554: PLAC. Since this reply is Pighian, and was formerly objected to our men, let Martyr refute it while I am silent, Commentary on Romans 5. 9. and Common Places, Class 2. chapter 1. section 8. Finally, he says, we have from Paul, that by the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners; which indicates that in those who are born of Adam there is a vice because of which they can be called sinners. But Pighius thinks he can elude this, because sinners are sometimes so called because of guilt although the act of sinning has passed and no longer exists.
555: Although this is so, yet he can never show from the Scriptures that anyone is called a sinner unless he either has vice in himself, or has certainly committed it before: unless he would say that God makes men guilty without some sin of their own. I confess therefore that those who are punished or oppressed by calamity are called sinners, but not before God, unless they themselves have either committed sin, or have it in themselves: And truly it is manifest that the Apostle is at this in this place, that he may teach that sin has truly been propagated into all humans, not however something which is not sin, but only a consequent of sin.
556: If the name of sin is not taken properly in this place, but figuratively, by that figure by which the antecedent is put for the consequent, how do the Orthodox argue from this place against Pelagius and Pighius? And, if it is taken properly, how is it at the same time taken figuratively?
